title: Turn recordings into a case
description: Understand evidence archiving, case collaboration and the difference between selecting media and building an export.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional warehouse team investigating an incident. Ordinary recordings expire, but these clips need follow-up. What does creating a case actually do?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: It groups selected recordings with the incident's details and queues them for copying to a configured Vault archive provider. That is different from starring a recording. The archive has its own retention arrangement, and the copy needs to succeed.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So we start from the relevant footage, not an empty folder and a hopeful name?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. Start from a recording, a focused recording search, the context player or a Watchlist event. Review the selected media before creating the case. This is an incident workflow, not a bulk archive for unlimited volumes of video.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The case is open. How does the team keep evidence and conversation together?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use the playlist for recordings, attachments for supporting files, and the details and comments for context. Assignees give people responsibility for follow-up. Labels and status help find and organise work as the number of cases grows.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Does approving or rejecting the case mean the same thing as its archive retention?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Status describes the investigation. The case's lifetime in Hub and the archived video's retention are separate settings. Decide both deliberately rather than expecting an Approved label to keep everything forever.

chapters.title: An export is a background build

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The team needs a bundle for a colleague. Is Generate export just another name for Download?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Generating queues a worker to build a bundle from the media and attachments selected for export. Download becomes useful after that build succeeds. The progress and freshness states tell you whether the bundle matches the current selection.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And changing the selected items doesn't quietly rewrite a bundle we've already built?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Correct. The existing export becomes stale and needs regeneration. Check both the selection and the finished status before handing it over. For older cases, the guide explains why all items may remain included rather than requiring a migration.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should the warehouse team check before sharing the case?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Review who should receive it and which recordings and attachments are selected for sharing. Export inclusion and share inclusion are separate choices. Also check the case's visibility and the permissions required to manage its membership.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose the relevant incident footage, confirm archiving, and make collaboration and retention explicit. When you need a bundle, generate and verify it. Use the linked guide for the exact sharing, permission and archive configuration details.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
